{{Short description|Partial order between random variables}}
{{Other uses|Dominance (disambiguation){{!}}Dominance}}
'''Stochastic dominance''' is a [[Partially ordered set|partial order]] between [[random variable]]s.<ref name="HadarRussell1969">{{cite journal |last1=Hadar |first1=J. |last2=Russell |first2=W. |title=Rules for Ordering Uncertain Prospects |journal=[[American Economic Review]] |volume=59 |issue=1 |year=1969 |pages=25–34 |jstor=1811090 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Bawa |first=Vijay S. |title=Optimal Rules for Ordering Uncertain Prospects |journal=Journal of Financial Economics |volume=2 |issue=1 |year=1975 |pages=95–121 |doi=10.1016/0304-405X(75)90025-2 }}</ref> It is a form of [[stochastic ordering]]. The concept is motivated in [[decision theory]] and [[decision analysis]] as follows. By standard decision theory, a decision-maker has a [[utility function]] <math>U(x)</math> that encodes their [[preference (economics)|preference]]s, and if the decision-maker needs to pick between several gambles, each gamble's outcome is a [[probability distribution]] over possible outcomes (also known as prospects), and can be written as <math>X_0, X_1, \dots</math>. Then, the decision maker should rationally pick the <math>X_i</math> that maximizes <math>\mathbb E[U(X_i)]</math>.

In more general cases, however, the decision-maker's utility function may be not exactly known, so the above procedure cannot take place. Nevertheless, if we know some partial details about the utility function, then this may be enough to conclude something of the form "any utility function <math>U</math> that satisfies the given constraint must satisfy <math>\mathbb E[U(X_i)] \geq \mathbb E[U(X_j)]</math>". In this case, we say that <math>X_i</math> "stochastically dominates" <math>X_j</math>. [[Risk aversion]] is a factor only in second order stochastic dominance.<ref name=":1" />

Stochastic dominance does not give a [[total order]], but rather only a [[partial order]]. For some pairs of gambles, neither one stochastically dominates the other, since different members of the broad class of decision-makers will differ regarding which gamble is preferable without them generally being considered to be equally attractive.

Throughout the article, <math>\rho, \nu</math> stand for probability distributions on <math>\R</math>, while <math>A, B, X, Y, Z</math> stand for particular random variables on <math>\R</math>. The notation <math>X \sim \rho</math> means that <math>X</math> has distribution <math>\rho</math>.

There are a sequence of stochastic dominance orderings, from zeroth <math>\succeq_0</math>, to first <math>\succeq_1</math>, to second <math>\succeq_2</math>, to higher orders <math>\succeq_n</math>, each one strictly more inclusive than the previous one. That is, if <math>\rho\succeq_n \nu</math>, then <math>\rho\succeq_{k} \nu</math> for all <math>k \geq n</math>. Further, there exists <math>\rho, \nu</math> such that <math>\rho\succeq_{n+1} \nu</math> but not <math>\rho\succeq_n \nu</math>. Each level of stochastic dominance corresponds to stronger assumptions about the decision-maker's utility function. The stronger these assumptions, the more pairs of gambles can be ranked.

Stochastic dominance could trace back to (Blackwell, 1953),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Blackwell |first=David |date=June 1953 |title=Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=265–272 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729032 |issn=0003-4851|doi-access=free |author-link=David Blackwell}}</ref> but it was not developed until 1969–1970.<ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Levy |first=Haim |chapter=Stochastic Dominance |date=1990 |title=Utility and Probability |pages=251–254 |editor-last=Eatwell |editor-first=John |location=London |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan UK |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-349-20568-4_34 |isbn=978-1-349-20568-4 |editor2-last=Milgate |editor2-first=Murray |editor3-last=Newman |editor3-first=Peter}}</ref>

==Statewise dominance (Zeroth-order)==

The simplest case of stochastic dominance is '''statewise dominance''' (also known as '''state-by-state dominance'''). The idea is that anyone who prefers more to less (i.e. has [[monotonic]]ally increasing preferences) will always (weakly) prefer a statewise dominant gamble. It is defined as

: Random variable <math>A</math> is statewise dominant over random variable <math>B</math> if <math>A</math> gives at least as good a result in every state (every possible set of outcomes).

In symbols, <math>P(A \geq B) = 1</math>. This is written as <math>A \succeq_0 B</math>. 

For strict statewise dominance, an extra condition is needed: <math>A</math> gives a strictly better result in at least one state. In symbols, <math>P(A \geq B) = 1</math> and <math>P(A > B) > 0</math>. This is written as <math>A \succ_0 B</math>.

Similarly, if <math>P(A = B) = 1</math>, then both <math>A \succeq_0 B</math> and <math>B \succeq_0 A</math>, so <math>A \sim_0 B</math>, and they are equivalent in the sense of statewise dominance.

For example, if a dollar is added to one or more prizes in a lottery, the new lottery statewise dominates the old one because it yields a better payout regardless of the specific numbers realized by the lottery. Similarly, if a risk insurance policy has a lower premium and a better coverage than another policy, then with or without damage, the outcome is better.

==First-order==
[[File:Normaldistdominance2.svg|thumb|<math>F_{B \sim N(0, 1)}(x) \geq  F_{A \sim N(0.75, 1)}(x) \forall x</math> <math>\implies B(black) \leq A (red)</math>]]
[[File:Normaldistnondominance2.svg|thumb|<math>F_{X\sim N(0, 1)}</math> und <math>F_{ Y \sim N(0.25, 1.5)}</math>, X and Y are not comparable through first-order stochastic dominance.]]

Statewise dominance implies '''first-order stochastic dominance (FSD)''',<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Quirk | first1 = J. P. | last2 = Saposnik | first2 = R. | year = 1962 | title = Admissibility and Measurable Utility Functions | journal = [[Review of Economic Studies]] | volume = 29 | issue = 2 | pages = 140–146 | doi=10.2307/2295819| jstor = 2295819 }}</ref> which is defined as:

: Random variable A has first-order stochastic dominance over random variable B if for any outcome ''x'', A gives at least as high a probability of receiving at least ''x'' as does B, and for some ''x'', A gives a higher probability of receiving at least ''x''. In notation form, <math>P [A \ge x]\ge P [B \ge x]</math> for all ''x.''
This is written as <math>A \succeq_1 B</math>. Similarly to the case of zeroth-order, <math>A \succ_1 B</math> requires the extra condition: for some ''x'', <math>P[A \ge x]>P[B \ge x]</math>.

In terms of the [[cumulative distribution function]]s, <math>A \succeq_1 B</math> means that <math>F_A(x) \le F_B(x)</math> for all ''x''. <math>A \succ_1 B</math> requires the extra condition: <math>F_A(x) < F_B(x)</math> for some <math>x</math>. 

If <math>A, B</math> are comparable according to first-order dominance, then <math>\forall x, F_A(x) \le F_B(x)</math> or <math>\forall x, F_A(x) \ge F_B(x)</math>. In both cases, we say that "the distributions of <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> do not intersect".

When <math>A, B</math> are comparable according to <math>\succeq_1</math>, [[Wilcoxon rank-sum test]] tests for first-order stochastic dominance.<ref>Seifert, S. (2006). Posted Price Offers in Internet Auction Markets. Deutschland: Physica-Verlag. Page 85, ISBN 9783540352686, https://books.google.com/books?id=a-ngTxeSLakC&pg=PA85</ref>

=== Equivalent definitions ===
Let <math>\rho, \nu</math> be two probability distributions on <math>\R</math>, such that <math>\mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[|X|], \mathbb E_{X\sim \nu}[|X|] </math> are both finite, then the following conditions are equivalent, thus they may all serve as the definition of first-order (weak) stochastic dominance:<ref name=":0" />
* For any <math>u: \R \to \R</math> that is non-decreasing, <math>\mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[u(X)] \geq \mathbb E_{X\sim \nu}[u(X)] </math>.
* <math>F_\rho(t) \leq F_\nu(t), \quad \forall t \in \R.</math>
* There exists three random variables <math>X\sim \rho, Y \sim \nu, \delta</math>, such that <math>X = Y + \delta</math>, and <math>\delta \geq 0</math>.
For strict first-order stochastic dominance, add a non-equality in the definition, as usual.

The first definition states that a gamble <math>\rho</math> first-order stochastically dominates gamble <math>\nu</math> [[if and only if]] every [[expected utility hypothesis|expected utility]] maximizer with an increasing utility function prefers gamble <math>\rho</math> over gamble <math>\nu</math>.

The third definition is equivalent to the second. The third definition states that we can construct a pair of gambles <math>X, Y</math> with distributions <math>\rho, \nu</math>, such that gamble <math>X</math> always pays at least as much as gamble <math>Y</math>. More concretely, construct first a uniformly distributed <math>Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)</math>, then use the [[inverse transform sampling]] to get <math>X = F_X^{-1}(Z), Y = F_Y^{-1}(Z)</math>, then <math>X \geq Y</math> for any <math>Z</math>. This then implies the second definition. The argument can be run backwards to show that the second definition implies the third.

=== Extended example ===
Consider three gambles over a single toss of a fair six-sided die:

: <math>
\begin{array}{rcccccc}
\text{State (die result)} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\
\hline
\text{gamble A wins }\$ & 1 & 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\
\text{gamble B wins }\$ & 1 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\
\text{gamble C wins }\$ & 3 & 3 & 3 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
</math>

Gamble A statewise dominates gamble B because A gives at least as good a yield in all possible states (outcomes of the die roll) and gives a strictly better yield in one of them (state 3). Since A statewise dominates B, it also first-order dominates B.

Gamble C does not statewise dominate B because B gives a better yield in states 4 through 6, but C first-order stochastically dominates B because Pr(B ≥ 1) = Pr(C ≥ 1) = 1, Pr(B ≥ 2) = Pr(C ≥ 2) = 3/6, and Pr(B ≥ 3) = 0 while Pr(C ≥ 3) = 3/6 > Pr(B ≥ 3).

Gambles A and C cannot be ordered relative to each other on the basis of first-order stochastic dominance because Pr(A ≥ 2) = 4/6 > Pr(C ≥ 2) = 3/6 while on the other hand Pr(C ≥ 3) = 3/6 > Pr(A ≥ 3) = 0.

In general, although when one gamble first-order stochastically dominates a second gamble, the [[expected value]] of the payoff under the first will be greater than the expected value of the payoff under the second, the converse is not true: one cannot order lotteries with regard to stochastic dominance simply by comparing the means of their probability distributions. For instance, in the above example C has a higher mean (2) than does A (5/3), yet C does not first-order dominate A.

==Second-order==

The other commonly used type of stochastic dominance is '''second-order stochastic dominance'''.<ref name="HadarRussell1969" /><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hanoch | first1 = G. | last2 = Levy | first2 = H. | year = 1969 | title = The Efficiency Analysis of Choices Involving Risk | journal = Review of Economic Studies | volume = 36 | issue = 3| pages = 335–346 | doi=10.2307/2296431| jstor = 2296431 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rothschild | first1 = M. |author-link=Michael Rothschild | last2 = Stiglitz | first2 = J. E. |author-link2=Joseph Stiglitz | year = 1970 | title = Increasing Risk: I. A Definition | journal = [[Journal of Economic Theory]] | volume = 2 | issue = 3 | pages = 225–243 |doi=10.1016/0022-0531(70)90038-4 }}</ref> Roughly speaking, for two gambles <math>\rho</math> and <math>\nu</math>, gamble <math>\rho</math> has second-order stochastic dominance over gamble <math>\nu</math> if the former is more predictable (i.e. involves less risk) and has at least as high a mean.  All [[risk aversion|risk-averse]] [[Expected utility hypothesis|expected-utility maximizers]] (that is, those with increasing and concave utility functions) prefer a second-order stochastically dominant gamble to a dominated one. Second-order dominance describes the shared preferences of a smaller class of decision-makers (those for whom more is better ''and'' who are averse to risk, rather than ''all'' those for whom more is better) than does first-order dominance.

In terms of cumulative distribution functions <math>F_\rho</math> and <math>F_\nu</math>, <math>\rho</math> is second-order stochastically dominant over <math>\nu</math> if and only if <math>\int_{-\infty}^x [F_\nu(t) - F_\rho(t)] \, dt \geq 0</math> for all <math>x</math>, with strict inequality at some <math>x</math>. Equivalently, <math>\rho</math> dominates <math>\nu</math> in the second order if and only if <math>\mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[u(X)] \geq \mathbb E_{X\sim \nu}[u(X)]</math> for all nondecreasing and [[concave function|concave]] utility functions <math>u(x)</math>.

Second-order stochastic dominance can also be expressed as follows: Gamble <math>\rho</math> second-order stochastically dominates <math>\nu</math> if and only if there exist some gambles <math>y</math> and <math>z</math> such that  <math>x_\nu \overset {d}{=} (x_\rho + y + z)</math>, with <math>y</math> always less than or equal to zero, and with <math>\mathbb E(z\mid x_\rho+y)=0</math> for all values of <math>x_\rho+y</math>. Here the introduction of random variable <math>y</math> makes <math>\nu</math> first-order stochastically dominated by <math>\rho</math> (making <math>\nu</math> disliked by those with an increasing utility function), and the introduction of random variable <math>z</math> introduces a [[mean-preserving spread]] in <math>\nu</math> which is disliked by those with concave utility. Note that if <math>\rho</math> and <math>\nu</math> have the same mean (so that the random variable <math>y</math> degenerates to the fixed number 0), then <math>\nu</math> is a mean-preserving spread of <math>\rho</math>.

=== Equivalent definitions ===
Let <math>\rho, \nu</math> be two probability distributions on <math>\R</math>, such that <math>\mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[|X|], \mathbb E_{X\sim \nu}[|X|] </math> are both finite, then the following conditions are equivalent, thus they may all serve as the definition of second-order stochastic dominance:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book
| last1=Mas-Colell | first1=Andreu
| last2=Whinston | first2=Michael Dennis
| last3=Green | first3=Jerry R.
| title=Microeconomic theory
| date=1995
| isbn=0-19-507340-1
| location=New York
|publisher=Oxford University Press
| at=Proposition 6.D.1
| oclc=32430901}}</ref>

* For any <math>u: \R \to \R</math> that is non-decreasing, and (not necessarily strictly) concave,<math>\mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[u(X)] \geq \mathbb E_{X\sim \nu}[u(X)] </math>

* <math>\int_{-\infty}^t F_\rho(x) dx \leq \int_{-\infty}^t F_\nu(x) dx, \quad \forall t \in \R.</math>
* There exists two random variables <math>X\sim \rho, Y \sim \nu</math>, such that <math>Y = X - \delta + \epsilon</math>, where <math>\delta \geq 0</math> and <math>\mathbb E[\epsilon| X -\delta] = 0</math>.
These are analogous with the equivalent definitions of first-order stochastic dominance, given above.

===Sufficient conditions===

* First-order stochastic dominance of ''A'' over ''B'' is a sufficient condition for second-order dominance of ''A'' over ''B''.
* If ''B'' is a mean-preserving spread of ''A'', then ''A'' second-order stochastically dominates ''B''.

===Necessary conditions===

* <math>\mathbb E_\rho(x) \geq \mathbb E_\nu(x)</math> is a necessary condition for <math>\rho</math> to second-order stochastically dominate <math>\nu</math>.
* <math>\min_\rho(x)\geq \min_\nu(x)</math> is a necessary condition for <math>\rho</math> to second-order dominate <math>\nu</math>. The condition implies that the left tail of <math>F_\nu</math> must be thicker than the left tail of <math>F_\rho</math>.

==Third-order==
Let <math>F_\rho</math> and <math>F_\nu</math> be the cumulative distribution functions of two distinct investments <math>\rho</math> and <math>\nu</math>. <math>\rho</math> dominates <math>\nu</math> in '''the third order''' if and only if both

* <math>\int_{-\infty}^x \left(\int_{-\infty}^z [F_\nu(t) - F_\rho(t)] \, dt\right) dz \geq 0 \text{ for all } x,
</math>
* <math>\mathbb E_\rho(x) \geq \mathbb E_\nu(x) </math>.

Equivalently, <math>\rho</math> dominates <math>\nu</math> in the third order if and only if <math>\mathbb E_\rho U(x) \geq \mathbb E_\nu U(x)</math> for all <math>U\in D_3</math>. 

The set <math>D_3</math> has two equivalent definitions:

* the set of nondecreasing, concave utility functions that are '''[[Skewness|positively skewed]]''' (that is, have a nonnegative third derivative throughout).<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Chan |first1=Raymond H. |last2=Clark |first2=Ephraim |last3=Wong |first3=Wing-Keung |date=2012-11-16 |title=On the Third Order Stochastic Dominance for Risk-Averse and Risk-Seeking Investors |url=https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/42676/ |access-date=2022-12-25 |website=mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de |language=en}}</ref>
* the set of nondecreasing, concave utility functions, such that for any random variable <math>Z</math>, the [[Risk premium|risk-premium]] function <math>\pi_u(x, Z)</math> is a monotonically nonincreasing function of <math>x</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Whitmore |first=G. A. |date=1970 |title=Third-Degree Stochastic Dominance |journal=The American Economic Review |volume=60 |issue=3 |pages=457–459 |jstor=1817999 |issn=0002-8282}}</ref>

Here, <math>\pi_u(x, Z)</math> is defined as the solution to the problem<math display="block">u(x + \mathbb E[Z] - \pi) = \mathbb E [u(x + Z)].</math>See more details at [[risk premium]] page.

===Sufficient condition===

* Second-order dominance is a sufficient condition.

===Necessary conditions===

* <math>\mathbb E_\rho(\log(x))\geq \mathbb E_\nu(\log(x))</math> is a necessary condition. The condition implies that the [[geometric mean]] of <math>\rho</math> must be greater than or equal to the geometric mean of <math>\nu</math>.{{Citation needed|date=December 2022}}
* <math>\min_\rho(x)\geq\min_\nu(x)</math> is a necessary condition. The condition implies that the left tail of <math>F_\nu</math> must be thicker than the left tail of <math>F_\rho</math>.

==Higher-order==

Higher orders of stochastic dominance have also been analyzed, as have generalizations of the dual relationship between stochastic dominance orderings and classes of preference functions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ekern |first1=Steinar |title=Increasing ''N''th Degree Risk |journal=Economics Letters |date=1980 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=329–333 |doi=10.1016/0165-1765(80)90005-1}}</ref>
Arguably the most powerful dominance criterion relies on the accepted economic assumption of [[Risk aversion#Absolute risk aversion|decreasing absolute risk aversion]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Vickson | first1 = R.G. | year = 1975 | title = Stochastic Dominance Tests for Decreasing Absolute Risk Aversion. I. Discrete Random Variables | journal = Management Science | volume = 21 | issue = 12| pages = 1438–1446 | doi=10.1287/mnsc.21.12.1438}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Vickson | first1 = R.G. | year = 1977 | title = Stochastic Dominance Tests for Decreasing Absolute Risk Aversion. II. General random Variables | journal = Management Science | volume = 23 | issue = 5| pages = 478–489 | doi=10.1287/mnsc.23.5.478}}</ref>
This involves several analytical challenges and a research effort is on its way to address those.
<ref>See, e.g. {{cite journal | last1 = Post | first1 = Th. | last2 = Fang | first2 = Y. | last3 = Kopa | first3 = M. | year = 2015 | title = Linear Tests for DARA Stochastic Dominance | journal = Management Science | volume = 61 | issue = 7| pages = 1615–1629 | doi=10.1287/mnsc.2014.1960}}</ref>

Formally, the n-th-order stochastic dominance is defined as <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fishburn |first=Peter C. |date=1980-02-01 |title=Stochastic Dominance and Moments of Distributions |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/moor.5.1.94 |journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]] |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=94–100 |doi=10.1287/moor.5.1.94 |issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

* For any probability distribution <math>\rho</math> on <math>[0, \infty)</math>, define the functions inductively:
<math display="block">F^1_\rho(t) = F_\rho(t), \quad F^2_\rho(t) = \int_0^t F^1_\rho(x)dx, \quad \cdots</math>
* For any two probability distributions <math>\rho, \nu</math> on <math>[0, \infty)</math>, non-strict and strict n-th-order stochastic dominance is defined as<math display="block">\rho \succeq_n \nu \quad \text{ iff } \quad F^n_\rho \leq F^n_\nu \text { on } [0, \infty)</math><math display="block">\rho \succ_n \nu \quad \text{ iff } \quad\rho \succeq_n \nu \text{ and } \rho \neq \nu</math>

These relations are transitive and increasingly more inclusive. That is, if <math>\rho \succeq_n \nu</math>, then <math>\rho \succeq_{k} \nu</math> for all <math>k \geq n</math>. Further, there exists <math>\rho, \nu</math> such that <math>\rho \succeq_{n+1} \nu</math> but not <math>\rho \succeq_n \nu</math>.

Define the n-th moment by <math>\mu_k(\rho) = \mathbb E_{X\sim \rho}[X^k] = \int x^k dF_\rho(x)</math>, then

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=|math_statement= 
If <math>\rho \succ_n \nu</math> are on <math>[0, \infty)</math> with finite moments <math>\mu_k(\rho), \mu_k(\nu)</math> for all <math>k = 1, 2, ..., n</math>, then <math>(\mu_1(\rho), \ldots, \mu_n(\rho))\succ^*_n (\mu_1(\nu), \ldots, \mu_n(\nu))</math>.

Here, the partial ordering <math>\succ^*_n</math> is defined on <math>\mathbb R^n</math> by <math>v \succ^*_n w</math> iff <math>v \neq w</math>, and, letting <math>k</math> be the smallest such that <math>v_k \neq w_k</math>, we have <math>(-1)^{k-1} v_k > (-1)^{k-1} w_k</math>
}}

==Constraints==

Stochastic dominance relations may be used as constraints in problems of [[mathematical optimization]], in particular [[stochastic programming]].<ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Darinka Dentcheva |last1=Dentcheva |first1=D. |author-link2=Andrzej Piotr Ruszczyński |last2=Ruszczyński |first2=A. |title=Optimization with Stochastic Dominance Constraints |journal=SIAM Journal on Optimization |volume=14 |issue=2 |year=2003 |pages=548–566 |doi=10.1137/S1052623402420528 |citeseerx=10.1.1.201.7815 |s2cid=12502544 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kuosmanen | first1 = T | year = 2004 | title = Efficient diversification according to stochastic dominance criteria | journal = Management Science | volume = 50 | issue = 10| pages = 1390–1406 | doi=10.1287/mnsc.1040.0284}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author-link=Darinka Dentcheva |last1=Dentcheva |first1=D. |author-link2=Andrzej Piotr Ruszczyński |last2=Ruszczyński |first2=A. |title=Semi-Infinite Probabilistic Optimization: First Order Stochastic Dominance Constraints |journal=Optimization |volume=53 |issue=5–6 |year=2004 |pages=583–601 |doi=10.1080/02331930412331327148 |s2cid=122168294 }}</ref> In a problem of maximizing a real functional <math> f(X)</math> over random variables <math> X </math> in a set <math> X_0 </math> we may additionally require that <math> X </math> stochastically dominates a fixed random ''benchmark'' <math> B </math>. In these problems, [[utility]] functions play the role of [[Lagrange multiplier]]s associated with 
stochastic dominance constraints. Under appropriate conditions, the solution of the problem is also a (possibly local) solution of the problem to maximize
<math> f(X) + \mathbb E[u(X) - u(B)] </math> over <math> X </math> in <math> X_0 </math>, where <math> u(x) </math> is a certain utility function. If the
first order stochastic dominance constraint is employed, the utility function <math> u(x) </math> is [[monotonic function|nondecreasing]]; 
if the second order stochastic dominance constraint is used, <math> u(x) </math> is [[monotonic function|nondecreasing]] and [[concave function|concave]]. A [[system of linear equations]] can test whether a given solution is efficient for any such utility function.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Post | first1 = Th | year = 2003 | title = Empirical tests for stochastic dominance efficiency | journal = Journal of Finance | volume = 58 | issue = 5| pages = 1905–1932 | doi=10.1111/1540-6261.00592}}</ref>
Third-order stochastic dominance constraints can be dealt with using convex quadratically constrained programming (QCP).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Post |first1=Thierry |last2=Kopa |first2=Milos |title=Portfolio Choice Based on Third-Degree Stochastic Dominance |year=2016 |journal=[[Management Science (journal)|Management Science]] |volume=63 |issue=10 |pages=3381–3392 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.2016.2506 |ssrn=2687104 }}</ref>
